name: Incommensurability
statement: Rival paradigms may share no common measure, so no neutral standard can rank them.
meaning: Incommensurability is the thesis that successive scientific theories or paradigms can lack a common measure, so that there is no shared, neutral standard or language by which to compare them directly and decide rationally between them. The term is borrowed from Greek mathematics, where it literally means having no common measure, as the side and the diagonal of a square have no common unit; the notion became controversial in 1962, when it was advanced, around the same time and largely independently, by Thomas Kuhn in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions and by Paul Feyerabend. Kuhn's incommensurability has several strands. Methodological incommensurability is disagreement about which problems matter and what counts as a good solution or a legitimate method. Semantic or taxonomic incommensurability is the shift in meaning of key terms across paradigms, so that words like mass, planet, or element do not straightforwardly translate; Kuhn later stressed that such incommensurability is local, confined to a few interconnected concepts, and involves a kind of untranslatability. Perceptual or observational incommensurability is the idea that proponents of different paradigms in a sense see the world differently, a change Kuhn compared to a Gestalt switch and to the theory-ladenness of observation. The upshot is that theory choice is not fully compelled by neutral evidence and shared rules. Kuhn insisted, however, that incommensurable does not mean incomparable.
mechanism: Incommensurability explains why the choice between rival paradigms is not settled by evidence and logic alone. On Kuhn's account, a paradigm shift changes more than beliefs; it changes standards, meanings, and even what practitioners take themselves to observe. Methodologically, competing paradigms need not agree on which problems a good theory must solve or on what counts as solving them, so there is no shared checklist against which both can be scored. Semantically, the central terms of the two paradigms shift their meanings and reference: Kuhn argued that Newtonian mass cannot simply be translated into Einsteinian mass, and that where Priestley saw dephlogisticated air Lavoisier saw oxygen, so statements framed in one paradigm cannot be exactly restated in the other, a local untranslatability of a cluster of interrelated concepts. Perceptually, because observation is theory-laden, the adherents of different paradigms bring different expectations and categories to the same phenomena, and in a sense practice their trades in different worlds, so they do not confront a common body of neutral data. Because the standards, the language, and even the observations are not fully shared, there is no algorithm, no neutral decision procedure, that must lead every rational inquirer to the same verdict. Yet Kuhn was emphatic that this does not make paradigms incomparable or theory choice irrational: comparison remains possible, and choice is guided by shared values such as accuracy, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness, even though these do not dictate a unique result.

examples.text: Like the side and diagonal of a square, rival paradigms may share no common unit by which to rank them directly.
Kuhn held that Newtonian mass cannot be translated exactly into Einsteinian mass, a case of semantic incommensurability.

variants.name: Local incommensurability
variants.text: Kuhn's mature view that incommensurability is confined to a few interconnected terms, not whole languages.

variants.name: Feyerabend's version
variants.text: A more semantic incommensurability tied to Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism and his slogan anything goes.

whyItMatters: Incommensurability is one of the most influential and contested ideas in the philosophy of science, central to Kuhn's picture of scientific revolutions and to debates about rationality, realism, and progress. By arguing that rival paradigms lack a fully neutral common measure, it challenges the comfortable assumption that theory choice is always a matter of applying shared standards to shared evidence, and it explains why revolutions can look, to their participants, less like a proof than like a conversion. The thesis reshaped the history and philosophy of science and spread into many other fields, wherever people speak of parties talking past each other for lack of a common framework. It also provoked enduring controversy, since it seemed to critics to threaten scientific rationality, progress, and realism, prompting charges of relativism that Kuhn firmly rejected, insisting that incommensurable theories remain comparable and that choice is guided by shared values. The debate it sparked, including Davidson's and Putnam's objections to the very idea of wholly untranslatable schemes, sharpened our understanding of meaning, translation, and cross-theoretical comparison.

working.text: set two successive paradigms side by side and look for a shared, neutral standard of comparison.
note disagreement in standards, shifts in the meaning of key terms, and differences in what is observed.
conclude that no algorithm compels the choice, while granting that comparison and reasoned judgment remain possible.

limits: Incommensurability has been sharply criticized, and its strong readings are widely rejected. If rival paradigms were wholly incommensurable, in the sense of being completely untranslatable and incomparable, then, critics argue, the thesis would be self-undermining. Donald Davidson, in On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme, argued that the notion of a totally alternative, untranslatable conceptual scheme is incoherent, since to recognize something as a scheme at all we must be able to translate it. Hilary Putnam pressed a self-refutation charge: if the terms of an old theory were genuinely incommensurable with ours, Kuhn could not describe them in our language, yet he manifestly does. Partly in response, Kuhn narrowed his thesis to local incommensurability, affecting only a small cluster of interrelated terms, and repeatedly denied that incommensurable means incomparable or that science is irrational, holding that cross-paradigm comparison and value-guided choice remain possible. The mainstream view today treats incommensurability as a matter of degree and as local rather than global. Historical dating and attributions, such as the roughly simultaneous, largely independent introduction by Kuhn and Feyerabend in 1962, reward care.
misreadings: Incommensurability does not mean that rival theories are incomparable or that theory choice is irrational; Kuhn insisted incommensurable theories can still be compared and that choice is guided by shared values. It is not global untranslatability but, in Kuhn's mature view, a local shift affecting a few interconnected terms. And it does not entail relativism, a charge Kuhn rejected, so treating incommensurability as incomparability, as wholesale untranslatability, or as proving relativism, misreads the thesis.
origin: The thesis, advanced by Thomas Kuhn and Paul Feyerabend around 1962, that successive scientific paradigms can lack a common measure in standards, meaning, and observation, so that theory choice is not compelled by neutral evidence and logic alone.

sources.text: The Incommensurability of Scientific Theories, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — incommensurability as the lack of a common measure between paradigms, its Greek mathematical origin, its introduction by Kuhn and Feyerabend in 1962, the methodological, semantic, and perceptual strands, local incommensurability and untranslatability, and Kuhn's denial that it means incomparability or irrationality.

Thomas Kuhn, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kuhn's incommensurability across paradigm change, the Newtonian versus Einsteinian mass and phlogiston versus oxygen examples, the absence of a neutral algorithm for theory choice, and Kuhn's rejection of the charge of relativism.
